stt_transcript: We will hear argument this morning in Case 25-579, Department of the Air Force v. Prutehi Guahan. Mr. Ghoshi? Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court, a permit application is not final agency action. It's a request to someone else to take action. Filing a permit application triggers a back-and-forth process whose outcome is, by definition, a moving target until a decision on the permit is issued. Treating an application as final would just lead to a multiplicity of suits throughout a permitting process, which I think defeats the whole point of the finality requirement. Now Respondent says that the application reflects some internal Air Force decision to continue these activities for the next three years if Guam issues a permit. But the if is precisely the kind of contingency that makes this not final. Respondent also points out that the application enabled the old permit's expiration date to be told or extended. But that is at most an incidental or indirect effect of the application, really, of Guam EPA's failure to rule on the application. The direct and appreciable legal consequences of that extension flow from the terms of the old permit, which Respondent has not challenged. Now Respondent's claim also fails on the merits. RCRA is a comprehensive statute specifically targeting hazardous waste and specifically specifying which environmental review must occur at each step of a reticulated permit process. Respondent's attempt to take all of NEPA and just shove it into the application stage is not only duplicative of RCRA's requirements, which are the functional equivalent, but inconsistent with RCRA's specification of when each of those requirements should occur through the permitting process. All of that said, I don't think you need to actually address the interaction of NEPA and RCRA in this case, because NEPA by its terms does not apply to non-final agency actions. And so if you agree with us, as I think you should, that the application is not final agency action, that would not only resolve the threshold issue in the case, it would also have the effect of resolving Respondent's claim on the merits here. I welcome the Court's questions. Is there any point in this process at which the Air Force has made a final, engaged in a final action? No, I don't think so. An application itself is not agency action. It's not final agency action. But when the permit is actually granted? The permit, of course, would be a final action of Guam EPA. Now, that's not an agency under the APA, but there is a separate judicial review scheme to challenge Guam EPA's issuance of a permit, and Respondent, if it meets the criteria for bringing such a claim, is welcome to bring such a claim if and when Guam EPA issues a final decision on the permit. So you're saying that there's no point at which the Air Force's decision can be challenged? Because even if Guam goes ahead and says, okay, you know, granted, you're saying you don't have to go forward with it. You could always change your mind. You could say, okay, now we're going to do something different. The Air Force's action is never final and therefore never reviewable. The application is never going to become final agency action, and there is no cause of action under NEPA itself. Congress didn't provide one. So any review would have to go through the APA, and I don't think the APA provides a cause of action for this application at any point in time. If Respondent wants to try to bring an ultra-virus claim, it can try and do that if it meets the high bar for it, but that is the option that Congress has specified for this kind of claim. Well, do they have a cause of action against, under Guam law, against the Guam EPA for its failure to demand a NEPA? Yes. They would have, well, let me be clear. Guam, there is judicial review of a Guam EPA permit decision, and if they satisfy the requirements for that, and the reason I'm hedging is because Yes, that's what I wanted to know.
